definition.text: A farming system, defined by the FAO, that protects farmland from loss and restores degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and a variety of crops.

facts.text: Its first principle, minimal soil disturbance such as no-till, keeps minerals in the soil and prevents erosion and water loss.
Its second principle, a permanent organic cover of mulch, shields the soil from rain and wind and builds organic matter.
Its third principle is diverse crop rotation, which breaks pest and weed cycles and improves water infiltration.
Farmers can save 30% to 40% of time and labour by not tilling.
Benefits come slowly: building organic matter takes years, and early years can bring financial losses.
Barriers include the high cost of special planting equipment and competition with livestock for crop residues.

title: Agri-environment schemes

definition.text: Programmes, compulsory for EU member states, that pay farmers to adopt environmentally friendlier methods to make up for the cost of changing.

facts.text: Farmers join voluntarily and commit for at least five years.
In 2009 they covered 38.5 million hectares, 20.9% of farmland in the then 27 EU states.
In 2012 the European Commission spent €3.23 billion on them, far more than the €39.6 million spent managing Natura 2000 sites.
Their aim shifted from protecting threatened habitats, to keeping wildlife on farmland, to improving services such as pollination.
A 2015 review found schemes that take land out of production did better at boosting species than in-production schemes.

conflicts.text: Agri-environment schemes became compulsory for every Member State under the Agenda 2000 (1999) reform.
conflicts.note: Conservation agriculture dates compulsory schemes to 1992 (b7bc0cacc0b0); Common Agricultural Policy places it in the Agenda 2000 (1999) reforms.

notes: No article of its own; mentioned on Conservation agriculture and Common Agricultural Policy.

title: Results-based agri-environment schemes

definition.text: Schemes that pay farmers for a measured environmental result, such as breeding birds or plant species counted, rather than for following set practices.

facts.text: Pure schemes pay only for outcomes; hybrid schemes also require some management actions.
They tend to raise farmer autonomy and tie payment clearly to conservation results.

notes: Described only in Conservation agriculture § Future development.

title: Agroecology

definition.text: The study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming systems, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment.

facts.text: The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement.
It is multidisciplinary, drawing on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history.
It studies agroecosystem properties such as productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability, at scales from a gene to the globe.
Unlike natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces governing agroecosystems.
Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are its three certified varieties; organics is practised in 188 countries.
Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue food sovereignty.
Researchers heatedly debate which model of agriculture or agroecology policy should support.

contested_note: Researchers debate which model of agriculture, including agroecology, policy should support.
